content.title: Key Takeaways
items: A Content Brief is not an outline, a keyword list, or a prompt — it's a structured specification defining why content exists, who it's for, what evidence supports it, what it must and must not claim, and what a writer or AI system should actually produce.
The Content Brief sits between research and content production: research answers "what do we know?", the brief answers "what are we going to create from that knowledge?"
A good brief explicitly distinguishes verified information from a content idea, an assumption, and an item still requiring verification — never letting these blur together.

Content boundaries (what must NOT be included — unsupported claims, guarantees, invented statistics, individualized professional advice) are just as important as content requirements, and are frequently the section skipped by businesses that later regret it.
The brief should stay simple enough for a founder-operated business to actually use — this is a lightweight governance tool, not a 50-page bureaucratic document.

A completed, approved Content Brief becomes a genuine control layer for content integrity — a reference point to check the final article against, not just a planning exercise that's forgotten once drafting begins.

content.content: A local business might have real research, genuine customer questions, a keyword list, and good source material — and still produce weak content, because nobody actually defined what the final piece was supposed to accomplish before writing began. Research gathers evidence. A Content Brief turns that evidence into a clear specification.

items.definition: A structured document that defines the purpose, audience, scope, evidence, content requirements, structure, risks, and success criteria for a content asset — completed before production begins.

content.content: What it is NOT: it is not the article itself, not just a title, not just an outline, not just a keyword list, not an AI prompt, and not a content calendar. Each of these is a different, narrower tool — a Content Brief sits above and informs all of them.

content.title: 3. Why Local Businesses Need Content Briefs

content.content: Small teams face practical risks: inconsistent content quality, repeated research, generic AI text, unclear review ownership, excessive revisions, and unverified claims slipping through. A Content Brief helps reduce every one of these problems by making explicit decisions before writing starts.

content.title: 4. The Relationship Between Research and Content Brief
5. Content Brief vs. Outline vs. Prompt

rows: Full specification — why, for whom, evidence, boundaries
Instructions for AI to generate text
Broad — goal, audience, research, risks, SEO
No — risks generic output without brief

content.content: For a founder-operated business, a lightweight 15-field version is enough to begin: Working Title, Business Goal, Audience, User Intent, Content Purpose, Key Questions, Core Answer, Required Info, Sources, Claims to Verify, Structure, Internal Links, CTA, Reviewer, and Update Requirements.

The complete Locatria Content Brief Framework includes Content Identity, Business Context, Audience, Intent, Research Summary, Content Requirements, SEO/GEO, Trust/Risk Boundaries, Editorial Tone, Conversion CTA, and Governance.
Ask directly: what business problem should this content solve? Define whether the piece explains a service, answers recurring questions, supports local visibility, or builds topical authority.
Answer clearly: Who is this for? What do they need? What do they already know? What decision are they trying to make?
A strong brief centers on one clear, specific question (e.g., "How can a local business make its business information easier for AI systems to understand?").
Expand the primary question into supporting sub-questions (What? Why? How? When? Who? Where? What to avoid?).
Define a preliminary, evidence-grounded conclusion answer upfront to guide the writer/AI.

content.title: Step 6 — Convert Research Into Content Requirements
Step 7 — Define What Must Be Included

content.content: List required definitions, workflows, tables, checklists, FAQs, and warnings to prevent essential content from disappearing during drafting.

content.title: Step 8 — Define What Must NOT Be Included

content.content: Define firm boundaries: no unsupported claims, no guarantees, no invented statistics, no unverified facts, no individualized medical/legal/financial advice.
Carry forward primary sources, secondary sources, URLs, dates, and verification statuses so writers do not rediscover research from scratch.

content.title: Step 10 — Define SEO and GEO Requirements

content.content: Specify primary topics, related concepts, entity references, user intent, and structured information without resorting to mechanical keyword stuffing.
Define introduction purpose, main section sequence, placement of examples/tables, FAQ location, and final takeaways.
Match the call to action to user intent (e.g., pointing educational guides toward related workflows or diagnostic checklists).

content.title: 24. AI's Role in Content Brief Creation

content.content: AI can help organize research, summarize findings, cluster questions, identify gaps, and format draft briefs. Humans must review and approve briefs before drafting begins.

content.title: AI Prompt Template: Content Brief Generator
content.prompt:
You are helping a local business convert research findings into a structured Content Brief.

RESEARCH FINDINGS: [insert research summary, sources, claims, evidence]
SOURCE LIST: [insert]
BUSINESS GOAL: [insert]
AUDIENCE: [insert]
PRIMARY QUESTION: [insert]
CONTENT TYPE: [insert]

Please generate a structured Content Brief covering identity, goal, audience, questions, core answer, requirements, boundaries, sources, SEO/GEO, structure, internal links, CTA, and maintenance.

Important: Do NOT invent facts, sources, or URLs. Preserve all qualifications.

content.title: 26. AI Prompt — Content Brief Quality Auditor
AI Prompt Template: Content Brief Quality Auditor
content.prompt:
You are auditing a Content Brief for completeness and quality before approval.

CONTENT BRIEF: [insert brief]

Assess: Completeness, Clarity, Research Support, Source Coverage, Audience/Question Specificity, Boundaries, Risks, Links, and Maintenance. Output result: PASS, PARTIAL, or FAIL with findings.

content.title: AI Prompt Template: Research-to-Brief Converter
content.prompt:
You are converting an approved research package into a Content Brief.

RESEARCH PACKAGE: [insert research, sources, claims, evidence, uncertainties]

Produce a complete Content Brief using only information in this package. Carry uncertainties forward explicitly; do not resolve them yourself.

content.content: A standardized markdown template detailing Content Identity, Business Goal, Audience, Questions, Core Answer, Sources, Required Content, Boundaries, Structure, SEO/GEO, Internal Links, CTA, Maintenance, and Approval.

content.title: 33. Content Integrity and the Content Brief

content.content: The approved brief serves as a reference benchmark for downstream validation: BRIEF vs. MARKDOWN vs. ARTICLE JSON vs. HTML.

items: Clear business goal and specific audience defined
Primary question and secondary sub-questions clear
Required content sections and formats defined
Sources, URLs, dates, and claim verification recorded
High-risk claims flagged and reviewer assigned
Approval status explicitly marked APPROVED before production

content.title: 10 Common Content Brief Mistakes
content.content:
1. Creating brief before research
2. Making brief only a keyword list or outline
3. Making brief too vague or overly complicated
4. Not defining audience, primary question, or core answer
5. Not recording sources or identifying risky claims
6. Letting AI invent missing info
7. Omitting content boundaries
8. Forgetting internal links or maintenance update triggers
9. Creating CTAs disconnected from intent
10. Producing content without brief approval

content.title: 39. What AI Can and Cannot Do

pros: Generate first-draft briefs and cluster questions
Identify gaps in research or brief specifications
Map research findings to content requirements
cons: Cannot guarantee factual, legal, medical, financial, or Fair Housing accuracy
Cannot replace human approval and domain expert review
Cannot guarantee search rankings, citations, or leads

items.question: What is a content brief?
items.answer: A Content Brief is a structured document defining the purpose, audience, scope, evidence, content requirements, structure, risks, and success criteria for a piece of content before production begins.

items.question: What is the difference between a content brief and an outline?
items.answer: An outline defines structural sequence. A Content Brief defines why content exists, for whom, based on what evidence, and within what boundaries.

items.question: Can AI create a content brief?
items.answer: AI can help organize research into a brief format, but human review and approval are mandatory before drafting begins.

items.question: How does a content brief support content integrity?
items.answer: It provides an explicit reference benchmark against which finished Markdown, JSON, and HTML can be validated for completeness and accuracy.
